name: Commenda
key_source: Harris; vault qirad notes. Extended 2026-08-18: van Doosselaere 2009, 64-68 corroborates AP3, LR1, LR3, LR4, CF1, CF2 and LR6 on the Genoese corpus, and Harris 2007, 11 describes the arrangement in Hansmann-Kraakman-Squire terms as a separate asset pool with 'asymmetric owners' shielding and an asymmetric entity shielding'. (i) DONE 2026-08-18 (ii): AP3 recoded 1 -> 0 and LR1 'limited' -> 'unlimited-several', after AP3 and LR1 were given an explicit locator (the labour-supplying party) and restricted to the venture's third-party creditors. The old values answered CF2's question. (ii) DONE 2026-08-30: the entity questions LP1-LP3, AP1, AP2, AP4, CI1-CI4 were asked and close three - LP1=0 (Harris 13, 'a nexus of contracts', with sole personal liability toward third parties at 10), AP1=P (Harris 11, the 'asymmetric entity shielding'), CI1=common (van Doosselaere 65, term 1's segregation clause). AP4=.NA on the no-founder disposition shared with bazacle_mill, casa_san_giorgio, the maone and partenrederij, WHICH LEAVES isqa AP4=0 AS THE ONLY SUBSTANTIVE AP4 ON A FORM WITH NO FOUNDER - see the adjudications, which recommend deciding AP4's locator on its own and then recoding all seven forms in one pass. The other six are .NR. PAGE CAUTION: Harris 2007 is an unpaginated conference draft and carries no printed page numbers; citations in this repo are to PDF pages, and the existing 'Harris 2007, 9' at AP3, LR1 and commenda_alloc RB2/RB3 points to PDF 10 in the held file. THE ENTITY FACET DOES NOT SEPARATE THIS ROW FROM societas_maris: the pair takes identical values on all ten, two of them on one shared datum. It separates only on LR6 and CF1, both WP1. PAIRED WITH societas_maris, added 2026-08-18 and coded on the same eleven cells. This row covers the UNILATERAL form; the bilateral form is the other row. CF3=bilateral here means TWO PRINCIPALS and is not the literature's 'bilateral commenda' - see the societas_maris CF3 note.

name: Societas maris (the bilateral commenda; Venetian collegantia)
key_source: ADDED 2026-08-18 as a new type row - the code did not previously exist in this vocabulary, though it does in loss_mitigation_type.csv, where it is now coded. van Doosselaere 2009, 64-68: the Genoese notarial cartularies, 6,764 commenda ties 1154-1315, 93 per cent of all coded maritime ties. p.65 states the two liability rules side by side - the unilateral investor 'bore all liability for loss' and the traveller 'bore no capital risk', while in the bilateral form, 'often called SOCIETAS IN GENOA', 'the liability for loss was proportional to the respective initial investments'. Contribution ratio customarily one third traveller, two thirds investor; profit split equally. Harris 2007, 9-13; Held 2025, 22 for the Ragusan contracts sharing lucrum and damnum in the same proportions. CODED ON EXACTLY THE ELEVEN CHARACTERISTICS commenda CARRIES, so the pair is comparable cell for cell. It separates on two: LR6 (symmetric against upside-only) and CF1 (P against 1). It agrees on AP3, LR1, LR2, LR3, LR4, LR5, CF2, CF3 and TS2. DISSENT, RECORDED NOT RESOLVED: Pryor 1977, Luzzatto 1961, 119 and van Doosselaere 2009, 65 n.7 all hold unilateral and bilateral commenda to be 'essentially the same agreement', the choice turning on the traveller's wealth. Every one of them reaches that on the PAYOUT, where the economics are identical by construction (the arithmetic is at 65 n.6). None reaches it on the loss. The row is kept separate because both of this project's datasets measure the loss. PERIOD NOTE: loss_mitigation_type.csv gives '10-13c' for the same code. That is probably too early for the Genoese evidence, which van Doosselaere's corpus opens in 1154, and the two rows should be reconciled at review. CROSS-DATASET LINK, WHICH cooccurs_with CANNOT EXPRESS: the same code is coded in loss_mitigation_forms (RB1=RB2=shared). check_vocabularies.py normalises the '@dataset' suffix away and then reads societas_maris@loss_mitigation_forms as a self-reference, so the link is recorded here in prose instead. STILL WANTED: Lopez & Raymond 174-184, where the contracts are translated - it would supply the quoted clause van Doosselaere paraphrases. Coded 2026-08-18; see logbook 2 and logbook 4 for that date. VENETIAN EVIDENCE ADDED 2026-08-18 (ii), and it tightens the period. Merelo-Guervos & Molinari 2025 (10.1007/s13278-025-01460-9, open access), on 381 Venetian contracts 1073-1342 from Morozzo della Rocca & Lombardo, Lombardo & Morozzo della Rocca, Bondi Sebellico and Tiepolo, identify the bilateral form AS the societas maris - 'the merchant supplying one-third of capital with equal profit division', which is exactly van Doosselaere's Genoese rule - and report that 'by the early thirteenth century, bilateral contracts had practically disappeared', the Tiepolo Statutes of 1242 regulating only the unilateral type. That matches van Doosselaere's 'the societas disappeared in the thirteenth century' in Genoa. THE EFFECTIVE WINDOW IS THEREFORE c.1073 TO THE EARLY 13c, NOT THROUGH THE 13c, and the '10-13c' on this row is too generous at the late end where it was suspected of being too generous at the early one. The period field on THIS row is set accordingly; loss_mitigation_type.csv still says '10-13c' and the two should be reconciled at review. ENTITY QUESTIONS ASKED 2026-08-30 and coded on the same ten characteristics as commenda, so the pair remains comparable cell for cell. It agrees with commenda on ALL TEN: LP1=0, AP1=P, CI1=common, AP4=.NA, and .NR on LP2, LP3, AP2, CI2, CI3, CI4. LP1 and AP1 are ONE DATUM SHARED WITH commenda, not two witnesses - Harris 11 describes the family and introduces the bilateral variant only at 12, where the sole stated effect is on profit-splitting - and both carry low confidence here against medium there, on the same reasoning as the 2026-08-18 AP3 and LR1 cells. CI1 is the one cell coded from a sentence naming THIS form: van Doosselaere 65, term 1, 'To the capital received, the traveler might also add his own capital ... in this case, the agreement was called a bilateral commenda' - one merged venture stock. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DISSENT RECORDED ABOVE: Pryor, Luzzatto and van Doosselaere 65 n.7 hold the two forms 'essentially the same agreement' on the PAYOUT, and this row was kept separate because both datasets measure the LOSS. The entity pass is the first evidence on the third question, entity STRUCTURE, and it finds no difference. NO COMPARATIVE CLAIM MAY TREAT THE PAIR AS TWO INDEPENDENT CASES ON ANY WP2 COMPONENT.

name: Mudaraba
key_source: NOT CODED HERE, AND THIS IS A DETERMINATION RATHER THAN AN OMISSION - the same disposition as ortoq_alloc in loss_mitigation_type.csv. Mudarabah is the HANAFI name for the institution coded in this dataset as 'qirad'. Ramli 2018, 97 on al-Sarakhsi's Kitab al-Mudarabah: al-Sarakhsi treats muqaradah as synonymous with mudarabah, 'the Malikites, Shafi'ites and Hanbalites unanimously use a different term i.e. qirad to denote such an activity', and 'in general, be it mudarabah, or muqaradah or qirad, it is by definition a commercial association whereby an investor or capital provider (rabb al-mal) entrusts some amount of capital to an agent... who trades with it and shares with the investor a pre-determined proportion of the profits'. Coding both rows would enter one institution twice and manufacture agreement between them on every cell. FALSIFICATION CONDITION, so this is not a permanent verdict. The schools are not known to diverge on any of the 32 characteristics, but one candidate is live and unverified: the vault note [[The mudaraba is revocable not locked in]] records that classical fiqh predominantly classifies the contract as an 'aqd ja'iz (revocable) while 'Maliki jurists restrict revocation once the agent has commenced work', flagged there as needing verification against fiqh sources. If that holds, mudarabah (Hanafi) and qirad (Maliki) separate on TS3 revocability - a WP2 capital-lock-in question, not a trivial one - and mudaraba earns a row. Note that qirad's own TS3 is currently uncoded, so the test cannot be run from what is in the matrix; it needs a Maliki source, which the library does not hold. Coded 2026-08-18; see logbook 2 and logbook 4 for that date.

name: Ortoq — equity regime (capital entrusted)
key_source: Enkhbold 2019 (Central Asian Survey 38:4, 10.1080/02634937.2019.1652799), 542-543, from Juvayni, Rashid al-Din and Vassaf. Principal bears losses capped at his investment, agent bears none — the qirad/commenda configuration. NOT A PHASE: Enkhbold has loan financing adopted 'when Ogedei and Mongke ruled', i.e. contemporaneous with the equity examples from Ogedei's own reign, so equity and loan are COEXISTING CONTRACT TYPES whose relative prevalence shifted, not a sequence. Dates deliberately left unperiodised. name: Ortoq — loan regime (capital advanced at interest)
key_source: Enkhbold 2019, 543-544, on Allsen 1989 and Otagi 1973. The second half of the split: ortoqs 'completely liable for the loans they took, which extended beyond partnership capital to their private properties'; guarantors unconditionally bound; on default, seizure and then enslavement of the defaulter and his family (Rashid al-Din 1998, 726). The isqa configuration. Attested from Ogedei's and Mongke's reigns and 'eventually became prevalent... by the end of the thirteenth century'. Enkhbold's stated cause for the shift in prevalence: the government spent 76,000 ding of silver in 1240 bailing out ortoqs, and 'the huge losses suffered by Mongol elites motivated Mongol authorities to shift towards a risk-transfer model'. NOT AN INDEPENDENT OBSERVATION from ortoq_equity.

name: Partenrederij / Partenreederei (fractional ship co-ownership)
tradition: Low Countries (Holland); the term reder migrated into German
period: 15c onward; coded on Hollandic law c.1619-1625
key_source: De ruysscher 2023 (Grotiana 44:2, 10.1163/18760759-44020002, open access), 334-365, and specifically 336-343 for the liability rules and 357-358 for the form itself: 'Ship co-owning associations had grown out of the co-ownership of ships. Such partenrederij had been used at least since the beginning of the fifteenth century. It was a fractional joint ownership, which allowed for pooling investments in costly ships.' CODED FROM ONE SOURCE, AND THAT IS THE FINDING ABOUT THE SOURCE BASE RATHER THAN A SHORTCUT. Of the five ship items in the Zotero collection 'HistorEE - beguinage and fractional ship ownership', only this one treats the Low Countries / German form: Haff 1910 is about medieval LAND and river transport cooperatives (Rott, Rottfuhren, carters' and boatmen's guilds - 121 occurrences of 'Rott' against 11 of 'Schiff', none of them about part-ownership) and contains no partenrederij material; Ebel 1975 is a two-page review of Ruhwedel, Die Partenreederei, with no attachment held and the book itself not in the library; Scammell 1962 and Steckley 2020 are ENGLISH part-ownership and are a different tradition - see the proposed-of adjudications, which recommend a separate type rather than folding them in. SCOPE: this row is the partenrederij STRICTLY - fractional co-ownership of the ship. De ruysscher 358 distinguishes it from the OPEN REDERIJ, in which 'the participants... were simple investors in a stock that was not the ship itself', and records that Grotius blended the two. Folding the open rederij in would make CI1 and CF1 span both values and require a split under the rule applied to voc on 2026-08-29. PERIOD AND EVIDENCE ARE NOT CO-EXTENSIVE, WHICH IS THE ROW'S MAIN WEAKNESS: the institution is attested from the early fifteenth century, but every coded liability cell rests on Grotius's Inleidinge (1619/1631) and De iure belli ac pacis (1625), and De ruysscher's own argument is that a general right of abandonment 'did not exist before Grotius put it to text' (350-351) and that Grotius 'stood on the sideline' of the development (363). AP3 and LR1 therefore carry low confidence. DESCENT CLAIM RECORDED, NOT ADOPTED: Gelderblom and Jonker (2004, 2010) make partenrederij a precursor of the voorcompagnieen and ultimately the VOC on continuity of fractional ownership and limited liability (356-357); Punt and de Jongh reject it, on the grounds that voorcompagnie participants had no right of abandonment and that voorcompagnie capital 'was not split up in portions, as was the case in the rederij' (357). The cooccurs_with link to the voc rows carries basis 'uncertain' for that reason. Note the repo's reserved terminology: any relation here would be PARALLELISM or descent, never 'convergence', since a shared ancestral condition is exactly what is in dispute. VAULT: no note on this form existed before this batch; the adjacent notes are on bodemerij, and [[The Bodmerei shield was a default rule and Amsterdam contracted out of it]] bears directly on AP3 and LR1 because its Amsterdam protests execute against the reders' persons and whole estates. Coded 2026-08-29 by ai; unreviewed.

name: Begijnhof / court beguinage (curtis beguinarum)
tradition: Low Countries (Southern Netherlands; also Lille, Valenciennes, Breda, Amsterdam)
key_source: Moran 2018 (Journal of Early Modern History 22:1-2, 10.1163/15700658-17-00010), 67-95, read in full - the single indispensable source, and unusually well matched to this matrix because its subject IS governance and financial administration. Its key structural statement, at 77: 'The Court Beguinages were internally divided into a standardized set of sub-institutions, each of which was financially independent from the others; these were the hof or court, the infirmary, the church, and the Table of the Holy Ghost... each sub-institution was legally a separate body and none could be held responsible for the others' debts.' Supported by Overlaet 2015 (in Single Life and the City, 1200-1900, 10.1057/9781137406408_7), 138-157, on the Great Beguinage of St Catherine in Mechelen from 40 beguine wills of 1532-91, and by Voigt 2012 (in Friedensnobelpreis und historische Grundlagenforschung, 10.1515/9783110259551.441), 441-476, on the legal status of the beguine way of life after the Council of Vienne in the dioceses of Cambrai, Tournai, Liege and Utrecht. SCOPE: THE COURT BEGUINAGE (begijnhof, curtis) ONLY. Moran 68 n.2 draws the line this row observes: the term was 'used to distinguish these large and consistently structured communities from smaller, less stable groups (begijngemeenschappen or begijnkonventen)', and 'whereas the Court Beguinages were incredibly stable ... the smaller beguine communities were far more transient'. Deregnaucourt 2000 in the same Zotero collection is about the hopital des Wetz at Douai - a couvent of about 27 beguines with an average stay of four years ten months - which is that contrast class, and is not coded here. It is in any case unreadable: its PERSEE PDF carries a text layer on the two cover pages only, the eighteen body pages extracting empty. PERIOD AND EVIDENCE ARE UNEVENLY MATCHED, AND THE ROW SHOULD PROBABLY BE SPLIT. Almost every entity-level coding here - LP1, LP2, LP3, CI1, TS4, MG2 - rests on Moran and is therefore post-1585. Three cells give positive evidence that the medieval position differed: TS4 (Moran 80 presents episcopal statute-making as a change that decreased the beguinages' autonomy), MG4 (Voigt 443, 475: a way of life following no supra-regionally binding rule, under no superior instance, 'nicht approbiert' yet held in high standing, its communities seeking Schutzprivilegien from secular rulers), and LP1 (Voigt 470: an Osnabrueck property transaction of 1320 requiring the consent of all 37 named beguines, in a community with no fixed enclosure and no hierarchy - though that community is a Domschwesternhaus and so the contrast class). A split at 1585 on the voc_1602/voc_1612/voc_1623 model is the obvious remedy and is NOT proposed in this batch, because on present sources both halves would rest on Moran and the split would manufacture agreement rather than test it. See the proposed-of adjudications. THE FORM'S CONTRIBUTION: LP3=1 is the first 1 on that characteristic in the matrix, and LR4=1 with LR5=diversifying is the third 1 and second 'diversifying' on the risk-pooling facet. Coded 2026-08-29 by ai; unreviewed. FALSIFICATION CONDITION FOR THE SPLIT, SO THE ONE-ROW DECISION IS NOT A PERMANENT VERDICT. The split at 1585 was considered and REJECTED for this batch, on the reasoning in the proposed-of adjudications: of the three cells that looked like medieval/early-modern divergence, LP1's counter-case (Voigt 470) is a Domschwesternhaus and therefore Moran's contrast class rather than evidence about the court form; MG4 would come out .NR on BOTH rows, since the dual secular-and-ecclesiastical subjection Moran reports at 79 as having 'always' obtained is matched in Voigt's medieval material by episcopal commissions under Cum de mulieribus alongside Schutzprivilegien from secular rulers; and TS4's medieval value is not established either, because Voigt 443 says no superior instance was competent in matters of law and form of life, which asserts that NOBODY could amend the rules rather than that the entity could. A split on present sources would also put 21 of 22 substantive cells on one side and leave the other nearly empty, which is the mudaraba situation - two rows resting on one source manufacture agreement rather than test it. THE STANDING CAUTION, WHICH IS THE REAL REASON FOR WAITING: 1585 is where the SOURCE BASE begins, not demonstrably where the institution moved. Moran's article opens in the 1580s because her archives do. Splitting there would encode a periodisation drawn from record survival into the matrix, where a later reader would take the difference between the two rows for a finding about beguinages. That 1585 is also a genuine watershed in the world - Revolt, Trent, the 1559 episcopal reorganisation taking effect, the bishops taking the right to appoint the beguinage priests - is not by itself a reason to split; the test is whether a CHARACTERISTIC moved. SPLIT THIS ROW WHEN a medieval source gives a cell-level value that differs from Moran's on any of: TS4 (who held the power to amend the statutes before the bishops claimed it after 1585); LP1 or LP2 (whether a medieval court beguinage held property as an entity - the Ghent foundation charters Moran mentions at 80 n.24, which gave the grand mistresses and momboren the right to appoint the priests, are the lead); or MG2 (whether the grand mistress was elected before 1585). Philippen, De Begijnhoven: Oorsprong, geschiedenis, inrichting (Antwerp 1918) is the acquisition that would settle it - Moran 68 n.2 calls it the foundational overview of the Court Beguinages and their institutional structures and cites it for election procedures and for the text of the 1588 Mechelen statutes - with Simons, Cities of Ladies (2001) alongside.
